GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 20) to amend the Government Railways Act,
Explain.

It will be remembered by those who were present during last session that an amendment was made to the Government Railways Act to make the procedure for the collection of damages for loss of any kind more in conformity with that provided for by the General Railway Act. I find that two or three clauses were left out of that amendment last year that should have been embodied in it in order to make it more in harmony with the General Railway Act. This is to remedy that difficulty.

The old Act gave the Exchequer court full jjower in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I desire to ask the hon. Minister of Railways if his attention has been called to an accident which occurred at a level crossing near Kingston on the 26th inst., by which two people lost their lives and a third was seriously injured; also if he is aware that some five or six years ago an award was made by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council respecting this crossing, with a view to having a subway constructed; and, if he is aware of such an order, will he call the attention of the Board of Railway Commissioners to it, with a view to having it carried into effect. I would also like to ask if, in view of the increasing number of fatalities such as Mr. OLIVER.
those mentioned in the papers of the 26th inst., it is the intention of the government to bring down legislation at this session effectually to safeguard the lives and property of the people of this country at level crossings.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways).
speechtext:
In reply to the very important question of my hon. friend, I might say that this question of level crossings is one of great interest, not only in this country, but in every country where there is rapid transportation by railway. It is becoming even more important in countries where there is rapid transportation not only by steam railways, but by a network of electric railways. In reply to my hon. friend's first question, my attention has not been called to the accident referred to other than by the report in the newspapers. I know the locality very well, and I understand, as my hon. friend says, that some years ago, perhaps earlier than he suggests, a decision was arrived at by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, before we had a Board of Railway Commissioners, ordering a subway to be constructed at that point. The cost was to be divided between the county, the railway company and I think the city of Kingston. The city of Kingston objected, as the crossing is outside the city, and the county took the position that it could-not afford to bear its share of the cost. The matter has been in abeyance ever since. I know from experience, and from having passed over frequently the locality, that it is a dangerous spot. There are five or six tracks, then there is the local train from Kingston together with the trains coming over the Grand Trunk Railway, and it forms part of the railway yard, thus making the crossing a very dangerous one.
My hon. friend asked the larger question, namely, how we propose to deal with the level crossings.
What was the nature of the privy council order ?

I have not heard the particulars of it. It was the division of cost that attracted my attention more than anything else and the obtaining of information as to why the order was not carried out. This large question of level crossings is one that must be dealt with. There are level crossings of course where there is practically no danger, being in long stretches of level country where every one can see for miles, or at any rate for a sufficient distance in each direction to protect himself against an on-coming train. But the situation has become somewhat changed from what it was some years ago. During the past ten years at least, the speed of trains has been increased to meet the public demand for rapid transportation, not only the express but other trains as well, and the

driver in any ordinary carriage is very easily deceived in judging the time it takes for an approaching train to reach him. Many a driver is apt to misjudge the time a running train takes to reach a crossing. A running train takes a very small period to cover a quarter of a mile, when it is running at a mile a minute ; and in this connection the public are not always blameless. We grow careless in crossing railway tracks, but this other question arises that in this as in many other cases, the public ought to be protected against themselves. It does not relieve the situation at all if we say that a man was killed on account of his own carelessness. If some provision could have been made to protect his life even against his own rashness, such protection certainly ought to have been afforded ?
This question has been engaging my attention to some extent because, being familiar by travel with almost every spot in Ontario where these accidents have occurred. my interest has been excited to a greater degree than it would be if they occurred in some remote locality. I have in my mind some crossings which are very dangerous. In driving, myself, I have stopped as much as one hundred yards from the track to listen if a train were coming because I could not see it at any distance. I have had communications in a confidential way and many conversations with the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, who, for a year or more, has been gathering data in this matter. The board have asked the different railways of Canada to give a map showing the various crossings on their line, laying particular stress on the dangerous ones, and also marking out specially these where people have actually lost their lives. But after we know all that, what is to be done ? That is what my hon. friend would like to know. He would like to know what is the position of the government in the riiatter. Well, I am not absolutely in a position to say what the government intends doing ; but perhaps the House will permit me just to say a word on the question without at all intimating that we have arrived at any decision.
The question of level crossings is one that involves five parties. The one most interested of course is the family to which death has come by an accident. The general public is deeply interested in having some protection at the dangerous level crossings. Then there are the municipalities, the provincial government and the federal government, and then there are the railways. In point of liability, perhaps we had better commence the other way. There are the railways, the Dominion and Provincial governments, the municipalities and the public.
And the railways.

Of course, they are the first on the list. The opinion of the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners is that, in a great many instances, the cost should not all be borne by the railways; and the commission has the power, under the Act, to provide, and has provided in some cases, that the municipality interested shall bear some of the cost. This much ought to be borne in mind with regard to the municipality, and I am speaking without having given that phase a great deal of consideration but only casually. The municipalities have erred possibly in having allowed the railways to establish a certain right within these municipalities themselves. One right which they have allowed to be established in many instances, and which never should have been given is the right to the water front. That having been done, the Board of Railway Commissioners have held, and not without some justice, that the municipalities which have done this ought to bear a portion of the cost. The municipalities are bound to be benefited, to a certain extent, by having the danger, which they allowed to be created, removed. Then why should the provincial government give any aid or assistance to the removal of the difficulty ? I am not trying to force the hand of any provincial government, but am merely pointing out these considerations to the House which may help us in dealing with the question when the time comes. Many of our steam railways have been constructed under provincial charters. Even when they have been taken over by the federal authorities, the beginning of the trouble was created by rights given them by provincial governments ; but outside of that, the provincial governments have the same deep interest in this matter that we all have. It will be asked why should the Dominion government assist? I am not saying that the Dominion or provincial government or municipalities ought to assist. I am merely pointing out some arguments which have been placed before me and which I think worthy of consideration. If it be held by the board, and with some reason, that the railways should not bear all the cost, somebody has to bear the balance of it. Would it not then be wise to consider carefully whether, in working out a scheme-if we want to make it a success, and not merely with the object of gaining a victory over the railway companies, and municipalities, or of their gaining a victory over us, but having for our sole object the remedying of the evil and the protection of the lives of the people-would it not be wise for us to consider the situation of the federal authority-not the government but the whole parliament-in this matter ? Would it not be worth our while to consider whether we ought not to join hands with the provinces and municipalities and create some fund out of which the expenses might be apportioned. so as to avoid quarrelling or

cavilling, or having a municipality refuse because the crossing was not in a city or because it could not bear that portion of the expense. We would then be in the position that when the Board of Railway Commissioners gave a decision ordering that so much be paid by the railways and so much by the province or municipality or Dominion, that order would be binding, and we would have this menace to public safety removed in a manner that would be satisfactory and not involve any great burden. This matter has been brought before me very hurriedly, and it is a very large question of which I am merely giving an expression of opinion in the hope that before the session closes we may come to a conclusion which will be satisfactory to all concerned.

Would the minister have any objection to bringing down the order that has been referred to, with any information available as to the respect, if any, in which it has not been carried out, and the reasons why it has not been carried out ?
That is, the order of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council?
Yes.
I will make a note of that and have it brought down.
I would suggest, also, that the minister should bring down not only that particular case, but all similar cases, in which the order has been made and not complied with. [DOT]

I would ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) if he will bring down the order in council in reference to the dredging. In answer to a question the minister said he would bring that down. I understood that he would be willing to do it without a motion.

Yes, without a motion. OPENING OF GOVERNMENT TENDERS.
House resumed adjourned debate on motion of Mr. J. D. Reid (Grenville):
That in the opinion of this House tenders received in any department of government should be immediately placed in safe custody under seal so as to prevent any possibility or suspicion of tampering; and should he opened in public at the time and place mentioned in the advertisement and in the presence of at least three principal officials of the department ; and the persons so tendering or their duly authorized agents should be at liberty to attend at the said time and place and see such tenders opened and recorded, if they so desire.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: At the hour of adjournment yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I was speaking of the affidavit, or alleged affidavit, to which my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) had referred, and which had been read by the leader of the New Brunswick government in a meeting held in the city of St. John. I stated to the House that that affidavit contained false statements of a most outrageous character, and statements which no public man ought_ to have read at a public meeting, reflecting upon the character of another person, whether that person were in public life or whether he were simply a private individual, without first having seen the person to whom the affidavit referred, inquired of him as to the fact and ascertained whether the statements were true or false. In a court of law, as every lawyer knows, even where matters of small moment are involved, before a party is allowed to read an affidavit, in ordinary cases, he is compelled by the rules to furnish a copy to the opposite party, so that that _ party may have an opportunity of answering.
Not unless it is demanded.

Whether it is demanded or not, the rules of the court provide that an affidavit should be served and notice given, so that the party concerned may have the opportunity to answer. But at this meeting to which I refer, Mr. Hazen, who is the leader of the Conservative party in New Brunswick, and who appeared at that meeting as leader-so that the Conservative party cannot shirk responsibility for his action-without notice to me and without having made any inquiry into the truth or falsehood of the" statements, read, upon the eve of the election, this affidavit involving a charge which, if it were true, would have damned me for ever in the eyes of the people of Canada, and, as I have said, would have driven me at once from public life. But, as I have said, the statements were absolutely false. The statement was that a public contractor, Mr. Gershon S. Mayes had, in October, 1907, after I had become Minister of Public Works, made a payment to me of $2,000, and coupled with the payment was the intimation on my part that it would be beneficial to Mr. Mayes to have a friend at Ottawa to look after his interests in connection with his contracts with the Public Works Department. Fortunately, the nature of this statement came to my knowledge almost at once, and I was able to show that, so far from my having received any money from Mr. Mayes, or having had any transactions with him at the time stated, the last money I had received from him was at a time two years before that, and long before I had become a member of this

House. It was at a time when I was acting as solicitor and counsel for Mr. Mayes, -and let me say that I had been his solicitor and counsel, advising him in important matters for a number of years before I received this payment from him. Well, as I stated yesterday, although I corrected this statement against me, and did what I could to have that correction sent broadcast over Canada (for I wished to put myself and the party to which I have the honour to belong right before the people of this country), yet-and I say this to the disgrace of the man who read that false affidavit and sought to do me that irreparable injury- he has never had the manliness to express regret for what he did; and the Conservative papers which published that false affidavit have never had the grace to express their regret for the false information they had given to the people. The reason why I asked my hon. frined (Mr. Foster)-who, let me say, has, in my opinion, done himself no credit by fathering this false affidavit and presenting it to the House-the reason, I say, why I was anxious to know whether he was aware whether an affidavit of the character he read is in existence or not is that I desired to know whether that affidavit was sworn to by the gentleman by whom it purports to be sworn to. I wanted to know whether that affidavit is in existence or not, for, if it is, it will be possible to found certain proceedings upon it, and if it is not in existence or has never been sworn to, this will not be possible. Through my solicitors, Messrs. Barnhill, Ewing & Sanford, I have made repeated applications for that affidavit. Application has been made to Mr. Hazen, who read it at the public meeting to which I have referred. He is, and was then, Attorney General of New Brunswick, and the Crown officer whose duty it would be to take action, if there had been any defrauding of the treasury of this Dominion, or any criminal offence committed, as has been suggested, by Messrs, Mayes and McAvity, or if I, as Minister of Public Works, had committed the crime so great as that charged in this affidavit. And what does Mr. Hazen say with regard to it ? He says that after reading the affidavit and making these serious charges, he surrendered the affidavit back to Mr. Gershon S. Mayes. But, though my solicitors have applied to Mr. Mayes he has declined to give it and has refused to answer letters addressed to him.
There is something further to which I wish to direct the attention of the House. For hon. members opposite have gone out of their way in this discussion, and have not confined themselves to the question whether it is or is not desirable to pass the resolution, but have dragged into this discussion matters relating to these dredging transactions in the 'city of St. John, and also matters relating to other contracts which 9
have been entered into by the Department of Public Works. And, that being so, it is desirable that I should deal somewhat more fully with this question than I would otherwise have felt warranted in doing. For, let me say, when the hon. members on the other side have read in this House the charges they have recklessly made throughout this country, when they insinuate that there has been graft in the conduct of affairs of the various departments of government, when they insinuate that the members of this government have not honestly and faithfully discharged their duties but have given favours to their friends, we are not only prepared to answer their charges but are prepared to carry on an aggressive campaign against them for their conduct in the elections through which this country has recently passed.
Now, Sir, what will be said of these extraordinary and outrageous affidavits? My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has stated that Mr. Mayes had entered into a contract with the Department of Public Works to perform dredging work in the harbour of St. John at 55 cents per cubic yard, which he intimated was more than it was really worth and more than Mr. Mayes would have been willing to do the work for. Upon that question let me invite the consideration of the House to this fact that later on public tenders were invited for work in the harbour of St. John of no more difficult character than that which had been previously awarded to Mr. Mayes and instead of tendering under public competition at 55 cents per cubic yard, which my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) intimates was too high a price, Mr. Mayes tendered at 90 cents and was the lowest tenderer, and was awarded the contract, with regard to which I understand no complaint has been made. After I had become Minister of Public Works, Mr. Mayes and Mr. McAvity requested me from time to time to relieve them from their 55 cent contract, claiming that the work was very hard and urging that as work had been given in the harbour of St. John to the Dominion Dredging Company also at 90 cents per cubic yard, the same price as Mr. Mayes had last tendered for in public competition, I should at least be willing to pay him for work which he claimed to be more difficult the sum of 90 cents per cubic yard. I refused to do that. I said to Mr. Mayes: You have entered into a contract and whether you gain or lose by it it is my duty to hold you to your bargain and I propose to hold you to your contract. Mr. Mayes also urged that, in addition to getting 90 cents instead of 55 cents per cubic yard, as under this contract he was getting only $5.60 per cubic yard for rock while under the new tenders, both he and the Dominion Dredging Company were getting $19.60 per cubic yard, which was claimed to be a reasonable



piice, he should at least be allowed $19.60 per cubic yard for the many large boulders which were being excavated at great expense. I refused his request and he became, as the correspondence which I produced before the electors will show, considerably annoyed, because he thought I was treating him harshly and not showing him that leniency he had a right to expect in view of the fact that contracts on easier terms had been let under public tender afterwards.
Later on Mr. Mayes came to the conclusion that he would like to get out of the dredging business and he made a proposal to me that if I would buy his dredge for my department at the price of $150,000 he would be perfectly satisfied and would abandon any claim. Associated with Mr. Mayes in this desire that my department should purchase his dredge was another gentleman very prominently connected with the Conservative party. I may say that Mr. Mayes is entitled to the credit of the virtue, if it be a virtue, of also being and having been for many years a prominent member of the Conservative party. Associated with him in this desire was his counsel, Aid. Baxter, of the city of St. John, who is vicepresident of the Liberal-Conservative Association of the city of St. John.

Is the hon. minister not aware that Mr. Baxter, to whom he referred, made a solemn declaration in which he denied emphatically that he had any pecuniary interest or any interest of any kind in connection with the dredge.
Yes.
And that he had no interest in Mr. Mayes whatever, except his interest as his solicitor and counsel.

That is entirely consistent with what I said. I said that associated with him in the desire that my department should purchase the dredge was Aid. Baxter, vice-president of the Liberal-Conservative Association of St. John. Upon one occasion, shortly before the election, 1 received a telegram which has also been made public, signed by Mr. Baxter, stating that his client was getting very impatient and urging me to close at once for the dredge, otherwise intimating that Mr. Mayes would make it unpleasant for me. I have forgotten the exact wording of the telegram, but that is its purport. That was followed by statements which were made to me by different friends, among them by Mr. Osman, a very prominent citizen of New Brunswick, formerly Speaker of that province, who came to me one day in a state of considerable excitement, because he is a true, a warm friend of mine, and has been so for many years, informing me that Mr. Mayes had told him of his desire to sell the dredge to the department, and that unless 1 purchased his dredge, disclosures would Mr. PUGSLEY.
very soon be made which would be of a most unpleasant character and would do great harm to the Liberal party and to the Minister .of Public Works. Among other things Mr. Osman told me that he had been shown a photograph of a cheque which Mr. Mayes had given in payment of this note to which I have referred, and Mr. Osman had been led to believe that this payment had been made to me after I became Minister of Public Works. When Mr. Osman told me what Mr. Mayes had said, I replied to him: Mr. Osman, did Mr. Mayes tell you that instead of getting this money after I became Minister of Public Works, I had received it from him for legal services when I was solicitor and counsel, and two years before I became a member of the parliament of Canada? He said: No, and I said: Tell Mayes to go ahead as fast as he pleases. I have nothing to fear and nothing to conceal.
What was the year in which the minister received the payment?
In 1905, nearly two years before I had become a member of the government.
You said two years before the party swore you had received it?

That is right, the party swore I had received it on the 15th of October, 1907, after I had become a member of the government and when I was Minister of Public Works and at a time when it would have been a crime, not merely a political crime but an actual crime of the worst character for me to have received money from a contractor having dealings with my department, but as a matter of fact the money had been received in October, 1905. I refused, as I said, to purchase the dredge, and the next thing which took place was that this affidavit was handed to the leader of the Conservative party in New Brunswick, who made himself the instrument of seeking to obtain vengeance for Mr. Mayes because I had declined to aCcede to his improper requests, and in the hope, as I have said, that he might do me irreparable injury. It has been said by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that it was explained that this was a typographical error. By a typographical error I understand is meant a printer's error. Would it not strike you, Mr. Speaker, as it struck the people of my own constituency and the people of New Brunswick, as an extraordinary thing that every Tory newspaper in Canada should have committed the same typographical error and that this affidavit, as it was published in all the Conservative papers throughout Canada, declared that I had received this money in 1907 after I had become Minister of Public Works. If you look at the news-

papers of that party you will find that it was discussed editorially all over Canada, and that it was intimated that the political days of the Minister of Public Works were about coming to an end. Afterwards it was stated not to have been a typographical error hut an error of the typewriter. But, as I have said, the most material part of this matter is that the Conservative party, through their leaders in New Brunswick, lent themselves to this unholy operation of seeking to destroy the character of a public man, and, put it in the best way you can, they were utterly reckless as to whether the allegation was true or false, and when it became known to them that they had done this great wrong to me, a wrong as great as ever was done a public man in this country before, they had not the manliness to express their regret for the conduct of which they had been guilty.
They did not even correct it.

No, as my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) says, they did not even correct it. But, fortunately if there is one characteristic of the people of New Brunswick which stands out more prominently than any other, it is that they love truth, they love justice and they love fair play. When the people realized what a despicable attempt was being made to win victory for the Conservative party they resented the course of hon. members opposite, or rather the associates of hon members opposite, in the province of New Brunswick, and by their verdict they showed that they did not approve of tactics of that kind.
I am not here to say that I had anything of great importance to do with the result in New Brunswick. I recognize, as our friends in this House must recognize, that it was the strong personality and splendid statesmanship of the gentleman whom we are all proud to follow that did so much in New Brunswick as it did all over Canada to ensure the success of the party. But, to me who had been made the representative of the province of New Brunswick, it was a great satisfaction that we were able to come back with eleven seats out of the thirteen to which New Brunswick is entitled in this parliament. It is a great satisfaction to me that we shall no longer be able to see our friend here who formerly represented the constituency of Kings and Albert, that our friend who formerly represented the constituency of Charlotte is also absent from the place which he occupied in this House and that our esteemed friend who formerly occupied the constituency of Queens and Sunbury is absent. The result in the province, of New Brunswick not only bears testimony to the confidence which the people of that province have in our great leader, but it is also an
evidence of the fact that they admire truth, justice and fair play.
Now, Mr. Speaker, hon. gentlemen upon the other side of the House have also, as a pretended reason for passing this resolution which has been moved by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) alleged that there has been graft and wrong-doing in connection with the receipt of tenders.
I endeavoured to show to the House yesterday why I think it is not in the public interest that tenderers should be invited to be present, at the opening of tenders. I think I satisfied the House that there is no good reason for departing from the coarse which it is admitted is pursued in the mother country, has been pursued ever since confederation in this country and has been pursued and is pursued to-day by the governments of the various provinces of Canada. I believe that every right thinking man in this House will agree that I am right in the view that if a public man, or a representative of the people, does not take the course which the people have the right to expect of their representatives, when they make insinuations such as were made here yesterday, if he does not avail himself of the opportunity of making and proving his charges before the committees of this House his allegations must be regarded as having no foundation. In this instance hon. gentlemen opposite have utterly failed to prove the insinuations which they have made. In so far as the opening of tenders for timber limits is concerned, the men who, of all others, could give the truth in regard to these tenders, proved before the committee last session that there was no irregularity in regard to them, that the tenders were received in a regular and proper manner and that the timber limits were awarded to the highest tenderers in every case. I say without hesitation, and I say it emphatically that it was proved before the committee at the last session of parliament, that it was stated in this House and that it was not denied. As far as the tenders which are received by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, by the Department of Public Works and by other departments of the government are concerned, it has not been shown that in any case there had been tampering with tenders, that any tender had been substituted for another, or that the lowest tenderers had been passed over except in special circumstances where the tenderers had been unable to carry out their contract or where they had previously failed to give satisfaction, and, as I stated yesterday, in every such case, the circumstances have }o be submitted to His Excellency the Governor General in Council and must be passed upon in council before the lowest tender can be passed over. Let me say to my hon. friends opposite that in every case where this course is adopted the reasons are set forth in the recommenda-
2C3

tion to council and it is open to the committees of this House and to any member of this House to have placed before either a committee of the House or the House itself the recommendation to council in which will be found stated the circumstances under which such a course is adopted. There is no secrecy about it ; every thing is open after the contract is once awarded and every paper can be brought down which any hon. member may desire to have brought down.
Now, my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middleboro) made a statement to this House yesterday and if he, with his eloquence, his fluency of speech and his apparent sincerity, repeated that statement from platform to platform in his own constituency, I cannot wonder why he is here as the representative of that constituency to-day because if the facts which he stated yesterday were true he would be able to make a strong appeal to the people of his constituency to withdraw their support from the government. What did the hon. gentleman say ? He said yesterday that very important dredging contracts involving large amounts had been let without tender, and that subsequently, upon complaint being made in this House, I had, instead of continuing these contracts, put them up to tender, and it had been claimed that a certain amount of money had been lost to the government by reason of doing it. That was the statement which my hon. friend made and it was an important statement. But let me say to my hon. friend that one very important matter in connection with it is that it lacks the essential element of truth.
The statement I made was that that was the statement which was made by the Liberals of that riding, and if it lacked the essential element of truth it was because they had made it.

I venture to say that my hon. friend's memory does not serve him as well as I would	like it to,
because I cannot conceive it possible that any Liberal member could have made that statement.	I have no
doubt that what the Liberal members stated was this: that there were certain dredging contracts which I as Minister of Public Works had the power to renew and which I had proposed renewing, but which by reason of protests made by gentlemen on the other side, Mr. Bennett among others,: and after I had given the matter consideration and remarked that the .forms of the previous advertisements rendered it somewhat doubtful as to whether the tenders were not limited to one season, I declined to renew them and again called for public tenders. I have no doubt that these Liberal members stated that as a result of calling for public tenders, in this way the

country was put to an expense of two or three hundred thousand dollars which it would not have been put to had I extended the original contracts. That, I assume, is the only statement which Liberal members made and that is the only statement they would be warranted in making. I cannot conceive it possible that any other statement was made by Liberal members in the constituency which my hon friend represents. These contracts which I was proposing to extend, I may say, had all of them been obtained after public tender in the first place and after keen competition. These were the facts which were before the Public Accounts committee. The tenders were produced before that committee and it appeared in every instance that the contracts had been awarded to the lowest tenderers, and that of course is a very different state of facts from that which my hon. friend (Mr. Middleboro) has presented to the House. Some gentlemen upon the other side of the House stated that Conservatives will not tender for dredging work because they feel they will not get fair play. Sir, I have yet to learn of any Conservative contractors in this country who hesitate to put in a tender to the Public Works Department. I have yet to learn the name of a single Conservative in this Dominion who claims he has been unfairly treated in connection with any tenders he may have put in to that department. I would ask my hon. friends opposite that instead of indulging in these insinuations-which do themselves an injustice as they do injustice to the members of the government; I would ask these hon. gentlemen to do me the fairness and to do the government the fairness of giving the name of a single Conservative contractor in Canada who says that his tender was improperly passed over or that he was improperly dealt with in the awarding of contracts under tender. In the most sincere way I invite hon. gentlemen opposite to do that. In the eyes of the people of Canada they must do it before they can expect the people to take any stock in the insinuations they make. Sir, il has been my pride since I have been a member of this government and in charge of one of the great spending departments, and I believe that it has been the pride of every member of this administration, so to conduct the affairs of his department as to do justice to every Canadian irrespective of his political leanings. The records of my department, and, I believe, the records of all the departments of the government, will show that this is the course we have pursued from the day we took office.
The commission did not say so.

The commission says nothing to the contrary so far as I remember, and if the commission does say anything to the contrary it can give no fact

upon which such a statement could be based.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I must ask the pardon of the House for having taken up so much time in the discussion of this matter. I have saidall I think it is necessary to say, but I do just want to make a reference to what has sometimes struck me as a most extraordinary thing, namely, that gentlemen in the Conservative party should think it so important that they should get possession of the reins of government as to deem it justifiable to resort to such tactics as I have described. Those of us who are charged with the duties of government have at best a hard task. Our work is not easy; our responsibilities are great; and while it is a great source of pride to be able to serve the public, yet it does seem to me that there is nothing in the position of a minister of the Crown, which should induce people to become lost to every sense of honour and of decency in order to reach that position. I have often wondered; I wondered in St. John when that false affidavit was read; I wondered the other day when the House learned that upon the eve of the election a forged telegram had been sent to British Columbia purporting to be signed by the leader of the opposition for the purpose of influencing the electors there to render a false verdict upon the issues on which the government was appealing to the country, what reason there could be to induce men to stoop to such things. It does seem that following the example of the leaders of the Conservative party in this House (and by that I mean all the members of the opposition), in indulging in insinuations and making reckless and unfounded charges of graft, their followers throughout the country were so desirous that the Liberal government should be ousted and the Conservative party come to power, that they seemed to feel that they were justified in resorting to any tactics, even to the reading of false affidavits and the forging of telegrams, to achieve their aim.
__ Mr. O. S. CROCKET (York, N.B.). Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in this debate and I would not have trespassed on the time of the House had it not been for the references which have been made by the Minister of Public Works to the so-called Mayes charges in connection with a dredging contract in the province of New Brunswick, and his further reference to the result of the elections in that province as a vindication of himself. It was to be expected that the Minister of Public Works would attempt to plume himself upon the success of the Liberal candidates in New Brunswick, but I am convinced that if the conduct of that campaign by the Liberals were fully exposed to this House and to the .public of Canada, the very unbecoming plumage with which the Minister of Public Works has adorned himself
would rapidly vanish. The great boasting of the Minister of Public Works about the results of the elections in New Brunswick would, I am satisfied, give place to chagrin and dismay if the truth were known in connection with the conduct of that campaign by the Liberal party. The fact is that the campaign as conducted by the Liberal party in the province of New Brunswick was one of the most discreditable that has ever occurred in that province. One of the first moves in that campaign was the purchase of two of the daily papers in the city of St. John, the Daily 'Telegraph' and the Daily 'Times' and the muzzling by that means of the entire press of the metropolis of New Brunswick. That consummation, I may add, was accomplished, I understand, by Mr. George McAvity and Mr. John E. Moore, two bosom friends of the Minister of Public Works, Mr. George McAvity being the very gentleman who got away with the $36,000 rake-off in connection with the contract that has been discussed on this motion. Mr. John E. Moore, I may say, is also now a contractor with the Public Works Department, and is, I understand, receiving under his contract fabulous prices for dredging in the province of New Brunswick.
Will my hon. friend allow me to ask him what are the prices which he says are fabulous?
The Minister of Public Works knows what the prices are.
I know they are not fabulous; I know they are reasonable.

There is no doubt that these gentlemen acquired the St. John 'Telegraph' on behalf of the Minister of Public Works. Perhaps the hon. minister will deny that he himself was associated with both of these gentlemen in the purchase of that newspaper property.
I will say that they are very excellent newspapers.

That was, as I have said, one of the first moves of the Liberal party in connection with the campaign in the province of New Brunswick. Then, we had the Minister of Public Works himself making the most reckless promises that were ever made by a Minister of Public Works throughout the province of New Brunswick. He promised, as I understand, in one speech in the city of St. John, to dredge out practically the whole of Courtenay Bay at a cost to this country, as was shown, of $5,000,000. That was only one of the promises which the Minister of Public Works made to the city and county of St. John. We had also the race and religion cry worked in the province to an extent that was unknown in the previous political history of that province, and in connection with the circulation by the Liberal party of

the pamphlet which has already been referred to in this House, entitled, 'The Duty of the Hour.' There were also employed in several, I will not say all, of the constituencies of the province of New Brunswick, the hugest corruption and bribery funds that were ever used in the constituencies of that province. In view of these facts, there is very little for the Minister of Public Works to boast of in connection with the result of the voting in New Brunswick. But, aside from the facts that I have mentioned, can that result be accepted by this House as a vindication of the Minister of Public Works with respect to this charge, or the many other serious charges which have been made against him in that province? What does he say as to the result of the voting in the city of St. John, where this affidavit and the counter affidavits were read?
Would you allow me to answer ?
No.

Does the Minister of Public Works deny that his colleague upon the ticket in St. John, Mr. Pender, was defeated, and that the seat for the city of St. John in this House is now occupied by our honoured friend Dr. Daniel ?
With a reduced majority of about 800.

But a majority nevertheless of the electors of the city of St. John, and notwithstanding the fact that the Conservative party had not one single newspaper in that city to put before the electors the issues of the day, and notwithstanding the promises which i have already mentioned of huge appropriations for public works in such a constituency, which we all know has for years been looking for such appropriations for the development of its winter port.
Where was the 'Daily Standard' ?

My hon. friend knows very well what the 'Daily Standard' was-a little poster that was published by the Liberal Conservative party, printed in a job office, and distributed throughout the city -a paper which of course could not get its matter before the electors as effectively as the old established newspapers. Now, Mr. Speaker, if there is anything in the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works with respect to the significance of the voting in New Brunswick, I think it is up to him to account for the verdict of the city of St. John, which went unmistakably against him.
In the city of St. John I obtained a majority of something like 300 or 350.

I am not able to speak as to that, because I have not examined the returns particularly ; but I do know that the Minister of Public W'orks appealed to the electors of the city of St. John to elect Mr. Pender, his colleague, and on one occasion he said that his vindication would not be complete if Mr. Pender were not elected with him. Mr. Pender was defeated, and the inference is that the verdict of the city of St. John was against the Minister of Public Works. Now, that is all that I think it is necessary for me to say in connection with the result of the elections in the province of New Brunswick.
With respect to the charges themselves, I do not intend at this time to go fully into them, because it seemed to me that this matter was rather suddenly precipitated into this debate, and perhaps rather irrelevantly. Such a matter cannot obtain in a debate of this kind the attention which its importance demands. It seems to me, however, that with such serious charges, characterized as serious by the Minister of Public Works himself, hanging over the hon. gentleman, it is the duty of this parliament to institute some sort of an investigation ; and when that investigation is had, the details can be discussed more profitably than at the present time. I want, however, to refer to the manner in which the Minister of Public Works has treated the question. It seems to me that he has passed over entirely the gravamen of the accusations which have been made in Mr. Mayes' affidavit. He has devoted practically the whole burden of his speech to an error in date which appeared in that affidavit. I wish now to call the attention of the House to the paragraph in the affidavit or solemn declaration of Mr. Mayes in which that error appeared, and I take this from the columns of the St. John ' Globe ' a Liberal newspaper.
A what ?
Does the Minister of Public Works say it is not a Liberal newspaper ?
I do not say any thing about it, I am asking you ?

I notice at all events that it figures in the Auditor General's Report for quite a respectable sum. Here is what Mr. Mayes says in his affidavit :
On October 15, 1907, I received a telephone message from Dr. P.ugsley, asking me to call and see him the next day, which I did. He said: Mr Mayes, I am in meed of money, and it would be nice if you could help ime.
I do not know whether that allegation is true or untrue.	[DOT]
I say it is absolutely false.

It has however a very characteristic sound :
I said, doctor, what for? You know that I have paid you some $1,300 in my second case against Conolly which you have in a way offered to pay me back because you have said that Mir. Emmerson was so slow in bringing up the matter, and I have not the funds. I am carrying a'big load and am paying large amounts to the Bank of -Montreal for over-drawais. Just then -Mir. Geo. iM-cAvity came in, and Dr. Pugsley said that Mr. Mayes' business was getting on so well that a little money would be very acceptable. I again said I was carrying a big -back load and that I could not eee why Dr. Pugsley should -ask me for money. 1 said: what do you want it for-a loan ? Well said Dr. Pugsley, you see it will be nice to have -some one who could do something -for you in Ottawa, there was always something -to he done, and if I could not give him a cheque, that I could give him a note for three or four months. After I was a minister. What is the actual time, do you say ?

I intend dealing with that. I have read the declaration with respect to the giving by Mr. Mayes of his note for $2,000, and I have read it as the declaration is printed. Mr. Mayes did not state in that declaration, as the Minister of Public Works endeavoured to lead this House to believe, that it was given to him when Dr. Pugsley was Minister of Public Works ; but there is no doubt in the minds of any one in the province of New Brunswick "that the date was an innocent mistake. I want, in this connection, to call attention to a subsequent declaration which Mr. Mayes made on the 14th of October, and which was widely published in the press, with respect to this alleged mistake, the House will then be able to judge what justification there was for the attack the hon. minister has seen fit to make on the honoured premier of New Brunswick. In a second declaration, sworn to before Mr. Beverly, R. Armstrong, signed by Mr. Mayes on the 14th of October last, Mr. Mayes says with reference to the date of this alleged interview :
I further say -that up to four o'clock iu the afternoon of the 12th instant, I had not given, or oau-sed to be given, to any member of the Conservative parity, any intimation that I was about to -make the declaration I did. During the afternoon I obtained an appointment with Mir. J. D. Hazen, to whom i submitted the matter, I further say -that when Mr. Hazen
read my declaration at the Queens rink, on the evening of the 13th, he turned towards m*, when reading the date '.16th October' and hesitated at ' 1907,' I called out ' 1905,' and he read ' 1905.'

Will my hon. friend allow me to ask him a question ? If it be true that Mr. Hazen's attention was called to the error in the date, how does my hon. 'friend reconcile that statement with the fact that Mr. Hazen read in public this affidavit, which appeared in the morning paper and was spread broadcast throughout Canada, with a false date in it ?
Does my hon. friend hold Mr. Hazen responsible for the printing of the declaration in the minister's own party papers ?
I do under these circumstances.

The hon. minister makes the statement that Mr. Hazen read that declaration with respect to this interview, in which the interview is stated to have taken place on the 16th of October, 1907, but surely Mr. Hazen, when he, in his reading, corrected the error, is not to be held accountable for the error which appeared in the papers the following morning. I think that the House will be able to judge pretty Well as to the value of the whole statement of the Minister of Public Works, with reference to the matter of these charges, by the manner in which he has dealt with this error in the date. He attacked the Premier of New Brunswick and the whole Conservative party for having entered into a heinous conspiracy to make this charge against him, as of a date when he was Minister of Public Works, and he said yesterday that there was not a Conservative newspaper in New Brunswick which had corrected that error. Let me say that there was not a Conservative newspaper in New Brunswick which I have read with reference to this matter, in which I did not see, the very day after the declaration was read, mention of the error which had been made, I also saw that it was corrected in the Toronto 'News', the ' Montreal Star ' and ' The Mail and Empire '. In every paper which I saw. I read of the mistake in the date which had been made, so that it looks very much to me as if the Minister of Public Works were endeavouring to draw the proverbial red herring across the trail. What I ask the House to bear in mind is the statement I have read as applying to the month of October, 1905. The Minister of Public Works says that this is the most infamous charge ever made against a public man in Canada. Perhaps in that statement he is correct, but does he say that the charge is very much less infamous as applied to him in October, 1905 ? He was then the Attorney

General of New Brunswick ; and if the statement of Mr. Mayes was correct, the Minister of Public Works was getting a rake off from a contract with the department of which he subsequently became a minister. That charge having been made -and I am not here to say whether the charge is true or not-as a member of this House and a citizen of this country, I am very much astonished that the Minister of Public Works should be content to rest under the accusation for four or five months without having instituted proceedings of any kind for the punishment of Mr. Mayes, who, he says, has done him*such a grievous wrong and whose charge, the minister himself says, if proved, would damn him for ever and drive him out of public life.

I do not wish to be misunderstood. I said that if it were true that I, after having become Minister of Public Works

Yes, that is what I said. If after having become Minister of Public Works and at the date given, October, 1907, I received moneys from a contractor having business with my department, I should be at once driven from public life-I should not be worthy to remain.

And I would ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), and I would ask also the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), if these charges made in this affidavit with the date corrected are true, is it proper that the Minister of Public Works should be retained in his position? This charge has never been retracted, with the exception of the correction of the date, it stands un-withdrawn; Mr. Mayes still insists upon it. And surely the Minister of Public Works who is one of the best lawyers in the maritime provinces and perhaps in the Dominion of Canada, ought to know that if Mr. Mayes, made a false statement in a solemn declaration, he is liable to prosecution for perjury.
_Mr. PUGSLEY. Yes, if you can get at his declaration; if you can find that which he has concealed and refuses to produce.

I am aware that the Minister of Public Works endeavoured to give the House the impression that the reason he took no steps in the prosecution of Mr. Mayes was that this declaration, as published in the St. John press, did not appear to have been signed. But has the minister the slightest doubt that Mr. Mayes signed that declaration? Was there not read in this House, yesterday afternoon, a letter by Mr. Mayes, addressed to the minister speaking of this solemn declaration as his affidavit ? Yet with such a letter in his hand the Minister of Public Works would still endeavour to Mr. CROCKET.
create the impression that he was unable to follow Mr. Mayes with a criminal prosecution. Furthermore as an able law-yer,-one of the ablest, as I have said, in the Dominion-he knows that Mr. Hazen, having read this declaration in a public meeting, if that statement were false, if any of these statements were false, he not only has an action against Mr. Mayes for perjury, but he has an action against Mr. Hazen for libel. Yet we have not heard, down to the present time, of any steps having been taken by the Minister of Public Works, or by anybody on his behalf, looking to the punishment of these gentlemen who have done him what he has characterized as the most grievous wrong ever done to a public man in the Dominion of Canada. The minister's course in this matter is in marked contrast with the course which he is alleged to have advised his predecessor in the cabinet from the province of New Brunswick to take in relation to certain other charges which did not involve that hon. gentleman's conduct in the administration of his department. Perhaps the Minister of Public Works has profited by the lesson which he taught his predecessor on that occasion.
Now, this allegation with reference to the giving of a note to the Minister of Public Works, when he was Attorney General of New Brunswick, in connection with this contract, is not the only serious allegation in that declaration. There is, to my mind, a more serious allegation than that, an allegation that more directly involves him as Minister of Public Works. The declaration states that, after the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) had become Minister of Public Works, after he had assumed control of this and all other contracts of the department, he sought to, and did, hold up Mr. Mayes in the interests of Mr. McAvity and the payment of this graft.

I desire to say to my hon. friend (Mr. Crockett)-and I say it in the strongest manner possible-and I am going to ask him now to accept my statement as a member of this House-that that is absolutely untrue, that I never held up Mr. Mayes, but that just as soon as the estimates of the engineer were put into the department in the ordinary course, and after the ordinary delays, the payment due to Mr. Mayes was made. The only exception was an amount of some $4,000 or $5,000, held back because Mr. Mayes had not performed his contract for cleaning out certain berths in the city of St. John which he had agreed to do in the contract with the city and for which my department had agreed to be responsible. With that exception, there was no holding back of Mr. Mayes' money. I will ask my hon. friend to accept my statement and not to read what I say is a false affidavit or persist in his statement.
I hope the hon. minister has not understood me as stating that this statement is true

I understand that. And I do accept it. I have no wish to do otherwise. But the question before the House is

As to that, I may say that I have allowed considerable latitude. I allowed the minister to speak a second time on a point of personal explanation. I do not wish to interrupt the hon member (Mr. Crocket) but I hope he will not go too far from the question before the House.

Reference to yourself?
Yes.

Now Mr. Mayes, I want you to settle up with. Mr. MeAvity and when that is done I will give you the balance.
That is one statement.

The hon. minister (Mr. Pugsley) said it was false and the hon. member (Mr. Crocket) must accept his statement, and cannot contradict it.

I do. I am not discussing the question of the truth or falsity of the charge, I am discussing the minister's pretext for not prosecuting Mayes for uttering that false statement. If that statement is not true, as the minister has alleged, why has he not proceeded against Mr. Mayes for making it? That was the very point I was discussing. Furthermore, if the minister would like any other ex-

tracts from the affidavit I would be glad to read them.

What I would say is that I do not think it is right, I do not think it is conducive to the dignity of the House or to good feeling in the House, that a member should read statements the truth of which he knows nothing about, particularly when another member makes the statement that what he has read is not true and I do unhesitatingly make the statement that what my hon. friend has read is absolutely untrue. It does seem to me my hon. friend should accept the statement.
He has accepted it for that, but there are others.
You had better read the other statements and get the minister's denial of them.

I accept the minister's statement, and the emphatic denial he has given this afternoon is the very reason why he cannot excuse himself for lying down under such serious accusations for six months and then attempting to convince the parliament of Canada that the reason he did not take the proceedings he should have taken was that there was no affidavit that purported to be signed. The affidavit from which I am quoting does purport to be signed, and the minister saw it published in the papers in St. John. He was fully aware of all the statements made in all these declarations. I do not think that

I was defending myself.

The hon. gentleman accused Mr. Hazen and Mr. Mayes of conspiracy, which is even worse than the accusation that was made against him,-certainly quite as bad. Minister of Public Works in connection with this matter and to discuss them alone. It is somewhat surprising that the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) should have sat through the speech of the hon. Minister of Public Works, to which he listened with such intense interest and admiration, without this point of order occurring to him, and that he should first be heard from in connection with points of order when I sought to rebutt some of the arguments which were addressed to this House by the Minister last evening and this afternoon.
I must say, however, Mr. Speaker, as I said at the outset, that I thought this matter was somewhat irrelevantly precipitated into this debate and as you have decided that it is not relevant to the motion which is before the House, any further observation I have to make I must, of course, confine to the question of the motion. I do not think it is necessary for me to say that I will very heartily support the resolution that has been moved by my hon. friend from Grenville. I think that instances have been given in this House, instances have been proved in the various committees which show the absolute necessity of some further safeguard being thrown around the reception of tenders and awarding of contracts. I have been somewhat surprised at some of the' statements which have been made by some new members who were not of these committees and by some old members who were of these committees, to the effect that there had been no instances in which there was any ground for suspicion in connection with the awarding of public contracts. But, it is not necessary now to rehash those instances. I am firmly convinced that the experience of the last eight or ten years has shown that there is an absolute necessity for greater care being exercised along the lines that are proposed in the resolution of my hon. friend from Grenville. I shall therefore have very great pleasure in recording my vote in favour of the resolution, and I know it is a vote that will be cordially approved by the people whom I have the honour to represent.

0. SEALEY (Wentworth). Mr. Speaker, in connection with the matter of doing public business it seems necessary to trust somebody to a moderate extent, and it would seem that the people of Canada have decided on the 26th October last to trust the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and

the able cabinet by which he is suround-ed. The amendment to the motion would seem to imply and provide for the least possible trust that could be imagined. That trust should be placed in the ministers in charge of the various departments, who are directly responsible to the department and who have been elected for the express purpose of assuming charge of public affairs. To entrust this duty to the minister and the chief officers of his department would seem to be as safe a plan as we could possibly adopt. It' would seem to be a practice along the line of British institutions generally as well as being in accordance with our system in Canada. But the motion, if I understand it aright, is intended to substitute the United States method of dealing with tenders whereby three officers of the department are present together with bidders or their representatives, or as many of them as care to be present. While the proposition of the hon. member who moved the resolution and of the other hon. gentlemen who support it may have the appearance of fairness, in actual practice what do we find? There is no place on the face of the earth where there is more newspaper or verbal complaint against the unfairness of the system and the generally unsatisfactory conditions of things that exist in the United States. It is true that in the United States tenders are opened by three officials of the department and as many bidders or their representatives as care to be present. But one of the officials generally attending is an office boy who cuts the paper envelope with a knife, another is an office boy who removes the bid from the envelope and another is a higher official who reads and announces the bid. After this is done the business generally lies in abeyance for about ten days. During that time the bidders are cognizant of whom their opponents are, and in many cases there are several bids in the same interest.
At the back of every bid there are about fifty conditions as to formality and if the powers that be should not award the contract to the lowest bidder it is returned to him marked 'informal.' I am satisfied that if _ the supporters of this motion could realize the millions of dollars that this system is costing the United States they would not be so enthusiastically in favour of it. So many are the conditions that there is scarcely any bid that cannot be thrown out by reason of informality, and if thrown out for informality, the securities are released and the_ bidders are relieved from the loss of their deposit or of their security to carry out the substance of their bid. The supporters of this motion are therefore trying to substitute for the British method which has worked so satisfactorily in this country, a system which has proved so iniquitous in the United States and which has been very costly to the government of that country.

I might say that the United States system encourages the practice of the bidders being represented by what are termed bidders' agents or bidders' brokers who earn their livelihood by that means, and whose conduct has led to grave irregularities. If the motion before the House were calculated to safeguard the public interest in any way it would be worthy of our support, but as the experience in the United States has proven that it is the very reverse I feel it is in the best interests of the country that I should support the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie).

Mr- W. S. LOGGIE (Northumberland, N.B.) Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up more than a very few moments of the time of the House. It seems to me that the real difference between the resolution and the amendment is whether the minister of a department is to be one of a number to open the tenders for the great works of this country. If any great corporation had a great work to be done and called for tenders, it seems to me that it would be reasonable that the president or managing director of that corporation should be_ present and see the tenders opened. Upon him is the responsibility for the proper management of the corporation's business. In the same way it is the duty of the minister, who is the responsible bead of the department, and in whom the confidence of the people has been placed, to be present and see that the tenders are opened in the regular way. Let me ask the hon. gentleman who moved this resolution: Do the Conservative Premiers of the Dominion of Canada ask that their representative heads of the several departments shall not be present as one of a number to see the tenders opened? Does Mr. Hazen in the province of New Brunswick say that the Commissioner of Board of Works shall not be one of a number to be present when tenders are opened? Does Mr. Roblin, does Mr. Whitney, does Mr. McBride, ask the legislatures of their several provinces to pass legislation that the minister, the head of the department, forsooth, shall not be present when tenders for works in his department are opened? It seems to me that the motion of my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid) is simply a motion of want of confidence in the government of the day; and surely, before he makes such a motion, he should ask his friends who lead the Conservative party in the several provinces what they are doing in this regard. It does seem to me that our affairs are quite as safe in the hands of the reresponsible heads of the different departments. My hon. friend said that there were not safeguards. Does he name a case? Is it insinuated that in the case of the Mayes contract, for example, there was tampering with the tenders? Such an insinuation, I understand, is not made, and therefore that particular ease is not relevant to the matter before the House, and cannot be pointed to as a reason for passing the original resolution instead of the amendment. In fact, had the original resolution been effective when that tender of 56 cents of Mr. Mayes and another for $1.25 from a firm in Ontario had been considered, no other result could have happened than did happen, namely, that the contract should be awarded to the lowest tenderer.

Now, I want to say only a word about the second clause of the resolution, namely, that the public should be present, or, if you like, those who tender should be invited to be present, when the tenders are opened. There may be something to be said in favour of that; yet there is another side to the story, and I think the Minister of Public Works was quite right when he said that it was possible that collusion might occur and that the interests of the public would not be safeguarded if that were done.
I have heard much to-day about the expenditure on public works in the city and county of St. John; but let me say for my own county that all contracts for public works there have been awarded to the lowest tenderer. Not only has this been the case with contracts for great public - works; but not one mail contract, during the four years that I have represented the county, has been awarded except to the lowest tenderer. I have a case in my mind of a tenderer for a mail contract who came to me and said, ' Can you tell me who has put in the next tender to mine, which is the lowest?' As I was not familiar with the ruling of the department, I asked the question on behalf of my friend. What reply did I receive? This, Mr. Speaker:
' It is against the rules of the department to announce the tenders until the contract is entered into.' My friend, I suppose, had an object. I merely propose making but a few short remarks, as I do not wish to take up the time of the House. The hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) suggested, in his opening remarks yesterday, that some method ought to be adopted to shorten the sessions of this House. In that I quite agree with him. I do think that some method might properly be adopted which will get us away from here in less than seven or eight months, but I do not think it was consistent with this suggestion that the gentleman should immediately have proceeded to take up the time of the House in discussing a suggested remedy for an evil which is purely imaginary. In my opinion the mode of letting contracts by tender is much the same to-day as it has been since confederation. The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart), who was formerly a cabinet minister himself, says that when the Conservative party were in power, no evil resulted from the method then followed. The Minister of Public Works tells us with equal earnestness that no evil exists and no wrong has resulted from the continuance of just the same method by the party now in power. It seems to me that we are bound to accept the statements of these two gentlemen until some proof be brought forward that they are not well founded. If there were that measure of evil resulting which is complained of by our hon. friends opposite, if the allegation of the hon. member from North Grey (Mr. Middleboro) be true that no Conservative contractor or

business man will tender to-day for government work, surely we would have heard of many complaints from them on that score. I observed, however, this afternoon that when the Minister of Public Works challenged our friends opposite to mention a single instance in which a Conservative had ceased tendering or abandoned what had been his business formerly, not one accepted the challenge. It may be true that there are complaints but from whom do they come? They come entirely, Mr. Speaker, from Conservative politicians, and not from business men. True my hon. friend from Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Boyce) gave one instance of a Liberal candidate having returned to his riding and told his people during an election campaign that he had been influential in getting for a local firm a certain portion of a public contract in that constituency, the member for Sault Ste. Oftentimes it would not be wise or proper, in fact, it would be most unbusinesslike, to award the contract to the man who puts in the lowest tender. The very fact that his tender is exceedingly or absurdly low would, of itself, be sufficient evidence that he would not be able to carry out and properly complete the contract. I remember a case in which tenders were called for a certain work. There were two tenders. But one of these tenders was so ambiguously worded that it was not certain whether the price did, or did not, include the heating for the building that was to be erected. If it included the heating, it was the lowest tender, but if it did not it was not the lowest tender. In such a case, I consider that the proper thing to do-and the thing that was done in the case I have referred to-was to get in touch with the man who put in the tender that was not understood and ascertain whether his tender did or did not include the heating. And, in fairness to all the parties who tendered, it was very important that the figures of the different tenderers should not, in the meantime, be made known to any one.
It will be remembered that the hon member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) said that all business must rest upon the trust that men have in men. But the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said that he was afraid that if we had such abundant faith in men, we would not, in the ordinary affairs of life, do our business very successfully, but would have to use a greater degree of caution. That, perhaps, is reasonable. I think that the hon. member for North Toronto may well set it as a gauge- that each of us may set it as a gauge-what would a man do in such a case if he were engaged not in public business, but in his own private affairs? A trustee, as I understand it, is expected to act as a prudent, intelligent, and honest business man would act if the circumstances were the same and he was handling his own affairs. Applying that to the matter before us, I would ask whether there are not many members of this House who have been members, it may be, of a church trustee board, of a school board, of an hospital board-and has any member of this House ever known any such case where tenders were called for and the tenderers were admitted when the tenders were opened? I have never known it to be so; and I do not think it is the custom for a man, in his own private business, when he has asked for tenders, to ask the tenderers to be present when tenders are openeed.
